A tryst is a secret, romantic meeting between two people — usually lovers — that is planned ahead of time and held in a private or hidden place, away from the knowledge of others.

That's the heart of it. But there's a lot of richness packed into this one small word, so let's unpack every layer.
The Four Core Elements of a Tryst

Understanding a tryst means understanding four things that are almost always present:

1. It's a meeting, not a place.
A tryst is the event of two people coming together, not the location itself. The meeting happens at a place, but the tryst is the meeting.

2. It's secret.
This is perhaps the most important quality. A tryst is not meant to be known by the outside world — not by family, not by friends, not by society. The secrecy is not incidental; it is central to what makes something a tryst. Two people who openly announce "we're going on a date tonight" are not having a tryst. Secrecy is its very soul.

3. It's romantic or intimate.
A tryst almost always involves two people who are in love, attracted to each other, or involved in a romantic or physical relationship. You would not use "tryst" to describe two friends meeting secretly to plan a birthday surprise, even though that is also a secret meeting. The word carries romantic weight.

4. It's planned in advance.
A tryst is not a chance encounter or an accidental run-in. It is arranged — the two people have agreed beforehand on when and where to meet. There is anticipation built into the word.

Beyond its definition, "tryst" carries a very specific emotional atmosphere. It feels:

  • Romantic and intimate — it evokes candlelight, whispers, and longing.
  • Slightly forbidden or clandestine — there is often a suggestion that this meeting is happening precisely because it shouldn't be, or because it must be kept hidden from someone who would disapprove (a jealous spouse, disapproving parents, a watchful society).
  • Literary and old-fashioned — you are far more likely to encounter this word in a novel, a poem, or a film than in everyday casual conversation. It has an elegance to it. People rarely say "I'm going on a tryst tonight" the way they might say "I'm going on a date." It belongs more to writing and storytelling.
  • Exciting and slightly dangerous — because of its secrecy, a tryst carries a thrill. There is something at stake. Getting caught is a real possibility, which raises the emotional temperature.
How It Differs from Similar Words

Tryst vs. Date: A date can be fully public and open — dinner at a restaurant, a movie, a walk in the park, all known to friends and family. A tryst is specifically secret. All trysts involve romantic meetings, but not all romantic meetings are trysts.

Tryst vs. Meeting: A meeting is completely neutral — it can be a business meeting, a school meeting, a meeting between strangers. A tryst is never neutral. It is always personal, intimate, and romantic.

Tryst vs. Rendezvous: "Rendezvous" is the closest word to "tryst" — it also means a planned meeting at a specific place. But "rendezvous" is broader; it can be used for military operations, business meetings, or spy handoffs. A tryst is exclusively romantic in nature.

• "She slipped out of the house at midnight for a secret tryst with the man she loved."
  • "The old stone bridge had been the site of their trysts for many years."
  • "He waited nervously at the garden gate, hoping she would keep their tryst."
  • "Their tryst was discovered when a neighbor spotted them leaving the café together."
  • "The letters revealed a passionate tryst that had lasted for nearly a decade."

Notice in each case: two people, a romantic connection, secrecy, and a planned meeting. All four elements are present.
When and How to Use It

Use "tryst" when you want to describe a romantic meeting that is secret and planned. It works best in written language — stories, essays, articles — or when you want to give your speech a more dramatic, literary flavor. It is not the kind of word you'd drop in a casual text to a friend.

You can say:

  • "a secret tryst" (common pairing, though slightly redundant since trysts are inherently secret)
  • "arrange / keep / have a tryst"
  • "their tryst"

To make sure the edges are crystal clear:

  • It is not a public date.
  • It is not an accidental or unplanned meeting.
  • It is not a meeting between friends, colleagues, or family members (unless there is a romantic dimension).
  • It is not a long relationship — it refers to a meeting, a single occasion (or a pattern of such meetings), not the relationship itself.
The One-Line Summary to Remember It

A tryst is a secretly arranged, romantic meeting between two people — intimate, hidden, and full of the thrill of the forbidden.

If you remember that image — two people slipping away from the world to be together, where no one else is supposed to know — you will never confuse or misuse this word.
